targets.title: Smart Radiator Valve vs Smart Thermostat: Which Comes First?

targets.chooseAlternative: Start with a compatible central thermostat, system balancing, or manual TRVs when the boiler control and basic room temperatures are not yet working correctly.

comparisonRows.alternative: Needs heating-system and wiring compatibility; manual TRVs avoid accounts.

comparisonRows.alternative: An unstable, unbalanced, or centrally uncontrolled system.

comparisonRows.label: Failure plan

targets.title: Smart Vents vs HVAC Balancing: Which Fixes Uneven Rooms?

targets.chooseAlternative: Choose balancing, duct repair, filter and return-air checks first when the cause of an uneven room is still unknown.
targets.decisionFocus: Do not use a motorized register as a diagnosis. Record supply and return paths, equipment type, minimum open-area requirement, thermostat location, room load, control behavior, and the manual position after power or network loss.

comparisonRows.alternative: Finds duct, return, filter, load, or equipment causes.

comparisonRows.alternative: Professional balancing works within measured system limits.

comparisonRows.label: Dependencies
comparisonRows.primary: Motors, batteries or power, sensors, hub and automation.
comparisonRows.alternative: Manual dampers, measurements, repairs and periodic service.

comparisonRows.label: Best sequence
comparisonRows.primary: A reversible final layer for a verified compatible system.
comparisonRows.alternative: The first action when room imbalance has not been diagnosed.

comparisonRows.alternative: Usually clearer when the monitored state matches the sensor type.

comparisonRows.alternative: Needs aligned magnets, angle, or a clean detection field.

comparisonRows.alternative: Freestanding or wall-mounted bins need stable placement outside the bath zone.

comparisonRows.label: Cleaning

comparisonRows.alternative: Rigid surfaces are easy to scrub but corners can retain residue.

comparisonRows.label: Best fit
comparisonRows.primary: Small lightweight toys and reliable hanging support.

targets.title: Outlet Caps vs Sliding Covers: Which Safety Layer Fits?
targets.alternativeOption: sliding covers or tamper-resistant receptacles
targets.searchQuestion: Should you use outlet caps, sliding cover plates, or tamper-resistant receptacles?
targets.choosePrimary: Use removable caps only when they fit tightly, remain intact, are reinstalled every time, and removed pieces are immediately controlled so they cannot become accessible small parts.
targets.chooseAlternative: Use self-closing sliding covers for frequently used compatible outlets, and ask a qualified electrician about tamper-resistant receptacles when the permanent electrical installation should provide the primary shutter layer.
targets.decisionFocus: No add-on makes an outlet harmless or replaces supervision and cord management. Inventory outlet and faceplate type, grounding and tamper-resistant status, daily plug frequency, cover fit, removal force, automatic return, furniture access, powered-cord exposure, heat or damage, small parts, local electrical requirements, and who restores protection after use.

comparisonRows.label: After use
comparisonRows.primary: An adult must reinstall and secure the cap every time.
comparisonRows.alternative: Sliding plates close automatically; receptacle shutters are built in.

comparisonRows.label: Small parts
comparisonRows.primary: A removed or damaged cap must never remain within reach.
comparisonRows.alternative: Fixed covers avoid loose caps but still need inspection.

comparisonRows.label: Installation
comparisonRows.primary: Fits only compatible unused receptacles and must grip securely.
comparisonRows.alternative: Cover plates or receptacles require exact fit and may need qualified installation.

comparisonRows.label: Primary plan
comparisonRows.primary: A supplementary barrier for selected unused outlets.
comparisonRows.alternative: Permanent protection plus inaccessible cords and active supervision.

targets.title: Corner Guards vs Edge Bumpers: Which Furniture Risk?
targets.alternativeOption: continuous edge bumpers or furniture relocation
targets.searchQuestion: Should you use corner guards, edge bumpers, or remove the furniture from the play area?
targets.choosePrimary: Choose individual corner guards when only a few hard protruding corners remain in an otherwise stable supervised area and each guard can adhere securely without becoming a detachable small part.
targets.chooseAlternative: Choose continuous edge protection when a long exposed edge is the measured impact path, or relocate the furniture when instability, climbability, glass, sharp hardware, failed adhesion, or repeated child removal creates a broader hazard.
targets.decisionFocus: Start by changing the room, anchoring required furniture, and removing avoidable hazards. Then map actual head and body paths, corner and edge profile, surface finish, adhesive compatibility, cure time, impact coverage, chewing, pulling, material damage, residue, cleaning, temperature, daily inspection, and immediate retirement after loosening or tearing.

comparisonRows.label: Coverage
comparisonRows.primary: Protects one protruding point with minimal added material.
comparisonRows.alternative: Covers a longer edge; relocation removes the contact surface entirely.

comparisonRows.label: Attachment
comparisonRows.primary: A small guard concentrates all retention on a short adhesive area.
comparisonRows.alternative: Long strips need uniform adhesion and can expose a longer loose piece.

comparisonRows.label: Room risk
comparisonRows.primary: Fits a stable item with a small isolated corner hazard.
comparisonRows.alternative: Use relocation for unstable, glass, climbable, or repeatedly accessed furniture.

comparisonRows.label: Inspection
comparisonRows.primary: Check every edge and corner for lift, tears, bite damage and residue.
comparisonRows.alternative: Apply the same inspection and remove any loose component immediately.

targets.title: Stove Knob Covers vs Kitchen Exclusion: Which Comes First?
targets.alternativeOption: removable knobs and active kitchen exclusion
targets.searchQuestion: Should you install stove knob covers or keep a child out of the cooking zone?
targets.choosePrimary: Use knob covers only as a supplementary layer when they fit the exact controls, withstand the appliance environment, let an adult shut off a burner immediately, and remain latched and intact under daily inspection.
targets.chooseAlternative: Use active kitchen exclusion, rear burners, turned-in handles, control locks where provided, or removable knobs when compatible because a knob cover does not block hot surfaces, cookware, climbing, gas leaks, or oven access.
targets.decisionFocus: Build the cooking-zone plan before selecting a cover. Verify appliance instructions, knob size and spacing, control markings, push-to-turn action, material heat limits, ventilation, adult emergency access, child reach and pulling, latch wear, cleaning, removed-part storage, gate and traffic path, supervision handoff, and what happens if a control is already on.

comparisonRows.label: Hazard covered
comparisonRows.primary: May deter access to compatible knobs only.
comparisonRows.alternative: Exclusion separates the child from controls, hot surfaces and cookware.

comparisonRows.label: Emergency use
comparisonRows.primary: Adults must see and turn every control off without delay.
comparisonRows.alternative: The cooking adult keeps direct access while controlling the child's zone.

comparisonRows.label: Compatibility
comparisonRows.primary: Needs exact size, spacing, action, temperature and appliance fit.
comparisonRows.alternative: Removable knobs and locks must be permitted; gates need a safe traffic plan.

comparisonRows.label: Primary plan
comparisonRows.primary: A secondary barrier inspected before every cooking session.
comparisonRows.alternative: Active supervision and exclusion remain the main control.
